chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'a, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
There is no zakat upon vegetables nor upon melons and their like, except what accumulates with you from their produce and remains with you for a year.

key_terms.الْبُقُولِ: Buqul - vegetables, leafy herbs, and garden plants; the term encompasses the broader category of perishable garden produce
key_terms.الْبِطِّيخِ: Battikh - melons, watermelons, and gourd-type fruits; used as a representative example of perishable garden fruits
key_terms.الْحَوْلُ / سَنَةً: Hawl/Sana - the one-year holding period required for zakat to become obligatory on most forms of wealth
key_terms.زَكَاةٌ: Zakat - the obligatory alms-tax, one of the pillars of Islamic practice; here specifically referring to zakat al-mal (wealth zakat)
key_terms.غَلَّتِهِ: Ghalla - produce, yield, or income generated from a property or commodity

ai.seo_question: Is zakat obligatory on vegetables and melons in Islamic law?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) issues a legal ruling that perishable agricultural products such as vegetables and melons are not subject to the zakat obligation. The exception applies only when such produce accumulates and remains in one's possession for an entire year, essentially converting it into a stored commodity subject to the standard hawl (one-year holding period) condition for zakat. This ruling reflects the Islamic jurisprudential principle that zakat on agricultural goods targets staple crops (grains, dates, raisins) and not perishable garden vegetables.
